title: The Vakataka Dynasty
description: An illustrated map of the Vakataka dynasty of the northern Deccan, from Vindhyashakti and Pravarasena I’s horse sacrifices through the Gupta marriage and Queen Prabhavatigupta’s regency, Pravarasena II’s new capital and the Nala raid, to King Harishena and the painted caves of Ajanta.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Vakataka Deccan, from about 250 to about 500 CE
note: Based on the Vakatakas’ copper-plate grants and cave inscriptions, excavations, the Puranas’ king lists and later poetry and tradition; each chapter says which it follows. Where the family began, how its kings are dated and what became of it are all debated. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

steps.title: Vindhyashakti and a lost homeland
steps.text: The Vakatakas’ own records begin with Vindhyashakti, whom the Puranas also name. An Ajanta inscription carved two centuries later calls him a Brahmin (dvija) whose power grew in great battles. Where the family came from is debated: some look to Bundelkhand in the north, others to Vidarbha, and an Amaravati inscription names a householder linked with the name Vakataka.
steps.today: Today: the Amaravati stupa site, Palnadu district, Andhra Pradesh.

steps.title: The only emperor
steps.text: Vindhyashakti’s son Pravarasena I is the only Vakataka called emperor (samrat) in the family’s grants. They say he performed four horse sacrifices (ashvamedha) and many other Vedic rites. The Puranas give a king Pravira sixty years at a city called Kanchanaka. Some identify it with Nachna in Bundelkhand; others doubt it, and his own capital is not known.
steps.today: Today: Nachna, Panna district, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: A marriage with the Bharashivas
steps.text: Pravarasena’s son Gautamiputra married the daughter of Bhavanaga, king of the Bharashivas. Vakataka grants praise them for carrying a Shiva emblem (linga) on their shoulders, bathing in Ganga water won by their valour and performing ten horse sacrifices. Coins of a Naga king called Bhava are found at Padmavati, and many identify him with Bhavanaga, but that is debated.
steps.today: Today: Pawaya, ancient Padmavati, Gwalior district, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Two branches
steps.text: After Pravarasena I, the kingdom split. His grandson Rudrasena I, son of Gautamiputra, led the main line in eastern Vidarbha. Another son, Sarvasena, founded a branch at Vatsagulma (Washim). Later writers credit Sarvasena with a Prakrit poem, the Harivijaya, now lost. The two lines ruled side by side for about a century and a half.
steps.today: Today: Washim, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A name on Samudragupta’s pillar
steps.text: On the pillar at Prayag, the Gupta emperor Samudragupta’s poet lists kings of the north (Aryavarta) whom he uprooted. One is Rudradeva. Some historians identify him with the Vakataka Rudrasena I; many reject this, since the Vakataka records show no break in his line. Either way, the Guptas were now the great power to the north.
steps.today: Today: the Allahabad pillar, in the fort at Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh.

steps.title: A Gupta bride
steps.text: Chandragupta II, Samudragupta’s son, gave his daughter Prabhavatigupta in marriage to Rudrasena II, grandson of Rudrasena I. Her mother, Kuberanaga, came from a Naga family. Many historians see the match as a Gupta move to secure the south before Chandragupta’s war on the Western Kshatrapas of Malwa and Gujarat. Where the wedding took place is not recorded.
steps.today: Today: Patna, Bihar, on the site of Pataliputra, and Nagardhan, near Ramtek, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The queen regent
steps.text: Rudrasena II died after a short reign, and Prabhavatigupta ruled for her young sons for at least thirteen years. Her copper plates found at Pune, issued from Nandivardhana, begin with her father’s Gupta line rather than her husband’s, and call her mother of the crown prince (yuvaraja) Divakarasena. He seems to have died before he could rule.
steps.today: Today: Nagardhan, near Ramtek, Nagpur district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A seal in the soil
steps.text: Nandivardhana is usually identified with Nagardhan, a village below Ramtek hill. Excavations there from 2015 to 2018 uncovered a settlement of the Vakataka age, and in it a clay sealing inscribed with Prabhavatigupta’s name, reported in 2019. Archaeologists took it as support for the identification, and as a sign of her standing at the court.
steps.today: Today: Nagardhan, Nagpur district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Plates from Ramagiri
steps.text: Long after her regency, in the nineteenth year of her son Pravarasena II, Prabhavatigupta granted land by a copper plate found at Riddhapur, issued at the feet of the lord of Ramagiri, a shrine on Ramtek hill. She calls herself mother of the kings Damodarasena and Pravarasena, perhaps one man. Vakataka-age temples still stand on the hill.
steps.today: Today: the temples on Ramtek hill, Nagpur district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A cloud from Ramagiri
steps.text: In Kalidasa’s poem the Cloud Messenger (Meghaduta), an exiled spirit (yaksha) on Ramagiri hill sends a rain cloud north with a message for his wife. Ramagiri is usually identified with Ramtek, though some place it at Ramgarh in Chhattisgarh. Tradition says Kalidasa visited the Vakataka court, perhaps as Chandragupta II’s envoy; nothing in the records confirms it.
steps.today: Today: Ramtek hill, which has a memorial to Kalidasa.

steps.title: A new capital
steps.text: Pravarasena II had the longest reign of the main line, and more of his copper plates survive than of any other Vakataka king. He founded a new capital named after himself, Pravarapura. Older scholars placed it at Paunar, near Wardha. Excavations at Mansar, near Ramtek, from 1997 uncovered a large temple complex, and some now place Pravarapura there.
steps.today: Today: the excavated temple complex at Mansar, Nagpur district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The bridge to Lanka
steps.text: A Prakrit poem, the Building of the Bridge (Setubandha), tells how Rama’s army bridged the sea to Lanka. It is attributed to King Pravarasena, usually taken as Pravarasena II, and the 7th-century writers Bana and Dandin praised it. A much later commentator says Kalidasa wrote it for the king, a claim most scholars doubt.
steps.today: Today: Paunar, on the Dham river near Wardha, Maharashtra, one candidate for Pravarapura.

steps.title: The only dated record
steps.text: In the Vatsagulma branch, King Devasena left affairs, an Ajanta inscription says, to his minister Hastibhoja. A stone inscription found at Hisse Borala records a lake named Sudarshana dug in his reign by one Svamilladeva. It is dated in the year 380 of the Shaka era, 458 or 459 CE, the only Vakataka record dated in a known era.
steps.today: Today: Hisse Borala, Washim district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The Nalas strike
steps.text: Under Pravarasena II’s son Narendrasena, the Nalas of Bastar seem to have struck deep into Vakataka land. A grant of the Nala king Bhavadatta was found at Riddhapur in Vidarbha, and many historians read it as a sign of conquest. Narendrasena’s son Prithvishena II is praised in his own grant for raising his sunken family again.
steps.today: Today: Riddhapur, Amravati district, Maharashtra; the Nala capital Pushkari is usually identified with Podagarh, Odisha.

steps.title: A vassal in the north
steps.text: Two inscriptions in Bundelkhand, at Nachna and Ganj, were set up by a ruler named Vyaghradeva, who says he meditates on the feet of the Vakataka Maharaja Prithvishena. Which Prithvishena is meant, the first or the second, is debated. Either way, the Vakatakas claimed a vassal far to the north, near Nachna’s early stone temple of Parvati.
steps.today: Today: the Parvati temple, Nachna, Panna district, Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: Harishena, lord of many lands
steps.text: Prithvishena II is the last known king of the main line. After him, Harishena of the Vatsagulma branch seems to have ruled both. An inscription in Ajanta’s Cave 16, given by his minister Varahadeva, son of Hastibhoja, says Harishena conquered Kuntala, Avanti, Kalinga, Kosala, Trikuta, Lata and Andhra. Many historians treat the list as a boast.
steps.today: Today: Cave 16, Ajanta, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The painted caves
steps.text: In Harishena’s time, nobles and monks cut new monasteries and prayer halls into the gorge at Ajanta and painted them. Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 hold the finest paintings: stories of the Buddha’s past lives (Jatakas), crowded courts and the bodhisattva Padmapani with a lotus. Cave 17 was given by a local king who served Harishena.
steps.today: Today: the Ajanta caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Work stops
steps.text: Many of Ajanta’s later caves were left unfinished. Cave 26, given by the monk Buddhabhadra, holds a great carving of the dying Buddha (parinirvana). The historian Walter Spink argued that nearly all this work was done in a short burst under Harishena and stopped soon after his death. Others spread it into the 6th century.
steps.today: Today: Cave 26, Ajanta, with its reclining Buddha.

steps.title: The end of the Vakatakas
steps.text: No record names a Vakataka king after Harishena, and the dynasty disappears from history about 500. In Dandin’s 7th-century prose romance (Dashakumaracharita), a good king of Vidarbha is followed by a pleasure-loving son who loses the kingdom; some historians read it as the Vakatakas’ fall. Kalachuris, Vishnukundins and later the Chalukyas took their lands.
steps.today: Today: Washim, Maharashtra.

steps.title: A tiger hunt in 1819
steps.text: In April 1819 John Smith, a British cavalry officer hunting a tiger above the Waghora river, saw a cave front in the gorge. He scratched his name and the date on a pillar in Cave 10. Copies of the paintings followed; many by Robert Gill burned in a fire in 1866. Ajanta became a World Heritage Site in 1983.
steps.today: Today: the Ajanta caves, with John Smith’s graffiti still in Cave 10.

items.name: Vindhyashakti
items.text: The first Vakataka named in the family’s records and in the Puranas. An inscription at Ajanta calls him a Brahmin whose power grew in great battles. Where he ruled, and how far, is not known.

items.name: Pravarasena I
items.text: The only Vakataka given the title emperor. The family’s grants credit him with four horse sacrifices and other great Vedic rites. His son Gautamiputra married a Bharashiva princess; another son, Sarvasena, founded the Vatsagulma branch. Gautamiputra seems to have died before him, so the main line passed to a grandson.

items.name: Prabhavatigupta
items.text: Daughter of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II and his queen Kuberanaga, she married the Vakataka Rudrasena II. Widowed young, she ruled for her sons for at least thirteen years, and her grants name her father’s line first. She was still granting land in the nineteenth year of her son Pravarasena II.

items.name: Chandragupta II
items.text: The Gupta emperor whose daughter Prabhavatigupta married into the Vakataka family. He went on to conquer the Western Kshatrapas of Malwa and Gujarat. Tradition links him with the poet Kalidasa, and with King Vikramaditya of later legend.

items.name: Pravarasena II
items.text: Son of Prabhavatigupta and Rudrasena II. He ruled for about thirty years, founded the capital Pravarapura and issued more surviving copper plates than any other Vakataka. The Prakrit poem the Building of the Bridge (Setubandha) is attributed to him.

items.name: Prithvishena II
items.role: Last known king of the main line
items.text: Son of Narendrasena. His grant praises him for raising his sunken family, usually read as recovering from the Nala invasion. He may be the Prithvishena whom Vyaghradeva of Nachna served. No later king of the main line is known.

items.name: Harishena
items.text: The last Vakataka king named in the records. His minister Varahadeva’s inscription in Ajanta’s Cave 16 claims wide conquests for him. Most of Ajanta’s famous later caves and paintings were made in his reign. What happened after his death is not recorded.

items.name: Varahadeva
items.text: Son of Hastibhoja, minister of King Devasena, he served Harishena as minister in his turn. He gave Cave 16 at Ajanta to the monks, with an inscription tracing the Vakataka kings, and his inscription also survives at the Ghatotkacha cave nearby.
